Another theory suggests that fortune cookies were born in California during the Gold Rush era, as a snack for miners and travelers (3). Veins, being blood vessels, contain oxygen-depleted hemoglobin, which absorbs and scatters light in a specific manner. The color we perceive when looking at veins is a result of this interaction between light and hemoglobin.

Now, let us delve into the physics of light scattering. When light enters human tissue, it encounters various obstacles, including collagen, elastin, and other biomolecules. These obstacles cause shorter wavelengths of light, such as blue and violet, to be scattered more than longer wavelengths, like red and orange. This phenomenon is known as Rayleigh scattering, named after the British physicist Lord Rayleigh, who first described it in the late 19th century.

In the context of veins, the blue color we observe is not due to the actual color of the oxygen-depleted hemoglobin, which is more of a purplish hue. Rather, it is the result of the selective scattering of blue light by the surrounding tissue. In contrast, longer wavelengths of light, such as red and orange, are able to penetrate more deeply into the tissue, reaching the vein itself, but are then absorbed by the hemoglobin, rather than being scattered back to our eyes.

Studies have consistently shown that the scattering of blue light is more pronounced in the epidermis, the outermost layer of the skin, whereas longer wavelengths of light penetrate more deeply into the dermis, the layer beneath. This is why veins, which are located in the dermis, appear blue, as the blue light is scattered back to our eyes, while the longer wavelengths are absorbed by the hemoglobin.

In conclusion, the blue color of veins is a result of the physics of light scattering, specifically the selective scattering of blue light by the surrounding tissue. It is not due to the color of the hemoglobin itself, but rather the way in which light interacts with the human tissue.
